$38 an Hour Is How Much a Year? $79,040 Full-Time, Before Taxes

Direct Answer$38 an hour is $79,040 a year full-time ($1,520 a week, $6,587 a month). See pay by period, overtime, unpaid weeks, and $64,435 take-home after federal tax.

Gross pay estimates

Quick Answer

$38 an hour pays $79,040 a year on the standard full-time calendar: 40 hours a week, 52 weeks, 2,080 hours in all. Spread across the year, that is $1,520 a week, $3,040 every two weeks, and $6,587 a month on average, before taxes. A single filer who takes the 2026 standard deduction keeps $64,434.64 after federal income tax and FICA alone, or $5,369.55 a month. That is 81.5% of gross pay, or $30.98 kept from every hour worked. Three details under the headline matter more than the headline. Only $12,540 of your income is taxed at 22%. A $1 raise from this rate keeps exactly $1,463.28. And an $80,000 salary sits just $960 a year ahead, a gap that 17 overtime hours close.

Saving $10,000 on $38 an Hour: The Honest Timeline

A $10,000 savings goal sounds simple until you price it against a real paycheck. At $38 an hour, federal-only take-home is $5,369.55 a month. Here is how long the goal takes at three savings rates, with no overtime and no raise:

You savePer monthMonths to $10,000
10% of take-home$536.9618.62
15% of take-home$805.4312.42
20% of take-home$1,073.919.31

The 20% row is the one to plan around. It sets aside $1,073.91 a month, or $495.65 from each biweekly check, and it reaches $10,000 in 9.31 months. In work terms, that goal costs 322.79 take-home hours, about 8.07 weeks of kept pay, not the 263.16 gross hours the $38.00 rate alone suggests. The 10% row stretches the same goal to 18.62 months, which is the honest price of a smaller habit. Two things shorten every row. Overtime pays $57.00 an hour, and each overtime hour keeps $40.10 after federal tax and FICA, so one overtime hour a week adds about $173.76 a month to the savings line. A $1 raise keeps $1,463.28 a year, or $121.94 a month, with no extra hours at all. Pick the row you can hold in a bad month, not the row that looks best in a good one.

The Short Answer: $79,040 a Year

The year comes from one multiplication. The take-home comes from three subtractions. These six steps all start from the same $38.00 rate used in every section below, so the whole guide runs on one set of rules:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Annual gross$38.00 × 40 hours × 52 weeks$79,040.00
Step 2 — Federal income taxTaxable $62,940.00: $1,240.00 + $4,560.00 + $2,758.80$8,558.80
Step 3 — FICA7.65% × $79,040.00 (SS $4,900.48 + Medicare $1,146.08)$6,046.56
Step 4 — Take-home$79,040.00 − $8,558.80 − $6,046.56$64,434.64
Step 5 — Per month$64,434.64 ÷ 12$5,369.55
Step 6 — Per biweekly check$64,434.64 ÷ 26$2,478.26

Start with Step 2, because it holds the detail most guides skip. The $2,758.80 comes from $12,540 of the $62,940 taxable income sitting in the 22% bracket. Run a flat 22% over the whole year and federal tax comes out $5,288.00 too high. The bracket-slice section below prices what that slice means for your next raise. One limit to keep in view: that take-home figure is federal only. It fits a single filer who takes the $16,100 standard deduction, pays no state tax, and has no 401(k) or health premium taken off. It also needs 40 paid hours in all 52 weeks, and no real year quite delivers that. The rest of this guide runs the same $38.00 rate through other schedules, overtime, and unpaid weeks, so you can find the number that matches your real year.

$38 an Hour in Every Pay Period

Same $79,040 year, six ways to slice it. Each row sets gross pay next to the federal-only take-home estimate, so find the row that matches the paycheck you actually get:

Pay periodHoursGross payFederal-only take-home
Hour1$38.00$30.98
Day (8 hours)8$304.00$247.83
Week40$1,520.00$1,239.13
Biweekly (every 2 weeks)80$3,040.00$2,478.26
Semi-monthly (twice a month)86.67 avg$3,293.33$2,684.78
Month (average)173.33 avg$6,586.67$5,369.55
Year2,080$79,040.00$64,434.64

The monthly row hides the first trap. It divides by 12, not by 4. Four weeks of pay is only $6,080.00, and the $506.67 gap is the extra 1.33 weeks an average month really holds. The second trap is the biweekly check itself. Biweekly pay means 26 paychecks of $3,040.00. Semi-monthly pay means 24 paychecks of $3,293.33. The two extra biweekly checks each year are what make the totals equal. A month with three biweekly checks pays $9,120.00 gross and $7,434.78 take-home. A normal two-check month pays $6,080.00 gross and $4,956.52 take-home. That swing is why biweekly pay feels lumpy. Our paychecks-per-year guide maps the three-paycheck months for every 2026 cycle, and our biweekly-versus-semimonthly comparison runs both schedules through a full year on the same salary.

What Overtime Adds

Federal law sets the floor. Under the Fair Labor Standards Act, non-exempt hourly workers get at least time and a half past 40 hours in a workweek. At $38.00 an hour, one overtime hour pays $57.00. Start with the pattern most people live, five extra hours a week, every week, and price it in full:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Overtime rate$38.00 × 1.5$57.00 an hour
Step 2 — Straight-time year40 hours × 52 weeks × $38.00$79,040.00
Step 3 — Overtime pay5 hours × 52 weeks × $57.00$14,820.00
Step 4 — Gross with overtime$79,040.00 + $14,820.00$93,860.00
Step 5 — Take-home with overtimeFederal $11,819.20 + FICA $7,180.29 off $93,860.00$74,860.51

Two warnings before the money. Overtime runs by workweek, never by pay period. A 45-hour week next to a 35-hour week still pays 5 overtime hours, as our timesheet guide prices in dollars. Five states add daily overtime on top of the weekly rule, and our daily-overtime guide maps them state by state. Now split the overtime money before you spend it. Of the $14,820.00, a full $9,880.00 is pay those hours would have earned at straight time anyway (5 × 52 × $38.00). Only $4,940.00 is the true premium, the extra half-rate (5 × 52 × $19.00). Take-home tells the same story. The overtime year keeps $74,860.51, which is $10,425.87 more than the $64,434.64 with no overtime, because $27,360.00 of taxable income now sits in the 22% bracket. Double the habit to ten overtime hours a week and the year pays $108,680.00 gross and $85,286.38 take-home. Our double-time guide shows the 2× version of this math, and the overtime calculator prices any pattern you type in.

What Unpaid Weeks Cost

The $79,040.00 headline needs 52 paid weeks. Unpaid time off takes weeks back out. Vacation without PTO, a seasonal gap, a slow January: each one comes straight off the year. The take-home hit runs bigger than the gross hit looks, because the weeks you lose are full-rate weeks:

Paid weeksHours paidAnnual grossFederal-only take-homeTake-home lost
52 (no unpaid time)2,080$79,040.00$64,434.64—
50 (2 unpaid weeks)2,000$76,000.00$62,296.00$2,138.64
48 (4 unpaid weeks)1,920$72,960.00$60,157.36$4,277.28

Four unpaid weeks cost $6,080.00 gross and $4,277.28 of take-home, yet that shorter year still beats a $60,000 salary by $12,960.00 gross and $9,767.36 of take-home. Two missing weeks cost $3,040.00 gross and $2,138.64 of take-home. That take-home loss beats the whole $37-to-$38 raise, worth $1,463.28 in the bracket-slice section. Keep that trade in mind when you weigh a job with unpaid gaps against one with paid time off. Now flip the comparison. A $38-an-hour job with two unpaid weeks pays $76,000.00 gross and trails an $80,000 salary by $4,000.00. The same job with all 52 weeks paid beats a $75,000 salary by $4,040.00. Paid weeks settle these comparisons. The headline rate does not. Our $37-an-hour guide and $36-an-hour guide price these same unpaid-week steps at their rates, so the three guides read as one ladder.

$38 an Hour After Taxes (Federal Only)

Here is the full bracket-by-bracket build for a single filer in 2026 who takes the $16,100 standard deduction. Every step is shown, so you can check it against your own pay stub:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Gross pay$38.00 × 2,080 hours$79,040.00
Step 2 — Standard deductionSingle filer, 2026− $16,100.00
Step 3 — Taxable income$79,040.00 − $16,100.00$62,940.00
Step 4 — 10% bracket10% × $12,400.00$1,240.00
Step 5 — 12% bracket12% × $38,000.00$4,560.00
Step 6 — 22% bracket22% × $12,540.00$2,758.80
Step 7 — Federal income tax$1,240.00 + $4,560.00 + $2,758.80$8,558.80
Step 8 — Social Security6.2% × $79,040.00$4,900.48
Step 9 — Medicare1.45% × $79,040.00$1,146.08
Step 10 — Take-home$79,040.00 − $8,558.80 − $6,046.56$64,434.64

Your marginal rate is 22%, yet only $12,540.00 of income is actually taxed at 22%, which is why the effective rate stays near 11%. Three numbers sum up the table. You keep 81.5% of gross pay. Your effective federal income-tax rate is 10.8% ($8,558.80 ÷ $79,040.00). Each hour worked keeps $30.98 of the $38.00. Watch one label on other sites. Several top-ranking pages call 18.5% the “effective federal rate” at this wage. That 18.5% mixes federal income tax and FICA together ($14,605.36 ÷ $79,040.00). Federal income tax alone runs 10.8%. State tax is the piece this sketch leaves out. Skip state income tax and the $64,434.64 stands. Add a state that taxes wages and it falls. Our paycheck-tax guide shows how to read the state line on your own stub, and our FICA guide splits the 7.65% into its two parts and the $184,500 wage base. Our paycheck calculator runs this same federal method on any rate and schedule, 401(k) included. A 401(k) contribution lowers the taxable income in Step 3. It does not lower the FICA in Steps 8 and 9.

Benefits can flip either row. The $12,540 Slice: What the 22% Bracket Really Costs

Other pages skip this section. It is the one that changes how you read your next raise. Your taxable income is $62,940.00, and the 12% bracket ends at $50,400.00. So $12,540.00 of your whole year is taxed at 22%, at a cost of $2,758.80, while the other $50,400.00 is taxed at 10% and 12%. That split is why your effective federal rate is 10.8% even though your marginal rate is 22%. Two results follow, and both are priced:

RaiseGross addedTake-home addedWhy
$36 → $37 an hour$2,080.00$1,463.28The whole raise is taxed at 22% + 7.65% FICA
$37 → $38 an hour$2,080.00$1,463.28Same again — the 22% bracket runs to $105,700 taxable
$38 → $39 an hour$2,080.00$1,463.28Same again — every $1 raise keeps $1,463.28 from here on

Price the common shortcut first. Tax all $62,940.00 of taxable income at a flat 22% and federal tax jumps to $13,846.80, a full $5,288.00 above the real $8,558.80. One top-ranking page makes a version of this error with a flat 25% tax and lands on $60,551.64 of take-home, $3,883.00 below the real figure. The raise math never changes from $32 an hour up: each $1 raise keeps exactly $1,463.28, which is $2,080.00 minus 22% federal ($457.60) minus 7.65% FICA ($159.12). That flat $1,463.28 holds until taxable income passes $105,700.00, which takes a gross of $121,800.00, or about $58.56 an hour. The last raise that kept more was $31-to-$32, at $1,665.28, because part of it still sat in the 12% bracket. Here is the choice that matters. Pick between a $1 raise and eight paid days off, and the days win on cash. Eight paid days at $38.00 pay $2,432.00 gross and about $1,710.91 of take-home, and not one dollar of it lands in a higher bracket. Our $37-an-hour guide and $36-an-hour guide carry this same ladder, so the $1,463.28 figure ties out across all three pages.

The $80,000 Salary Test: 17 Overtime Hours Close It

An $80,000 salary beats $38 an hour by $960.00 gross and $675.36 of take-home. No salary gap above this rate is smaller, and an hourly worker can close it in one afternoon. Overtime alone does it:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — The gap$80,000.00 − $79,040.00$960.00
Step 2 — Overtime hours needed$960.00 ÷ $57.0016.84 hours a year
Step 3 — Per week16.84 ÷ 52 weeks0.32 hours a week
Step 4 — The week that does it40.00 + 0.32 hours a week40.32-hour week
Step 5 — Take-home at $80,000Federal $8,770.00 + FICA $6,120.00 off $80,000.00$65,110.00

Round the math up and the rule fits in one line: 17 overtime hours a year, about twenty minutes a week, put the $38-an-hour year past an $80,000 salary, at $80,009.00 gross and $65,116.33 of take-home. One catch: those hours have to exist, and they have to be paid. Overtime you hope for pays nothing, and a salaried exempt worker gets nothing extra for the same late finishes. That trade is exactly what the hourly job wins. The next rungs take more work but still fit. An $85,000 salary leads by $5,960.00 gross and $4,192.86 of take-home, and 105 overtime hours a year (2.02 a week, a 42.02-hour week) close that gap too, at $85,025.00 gross and $68,645.09 of take-home. A $90,000 salary needs 193 overtime hours (3.71 a week, a 43.71-hour week) for $90,041.00 gross and $72,173.84 of take-home. Our $37-an-hour guide closes its $80,000 gap with 55 overtime hours, and our 5%-raise guide prices the other road to the same target. A raise to $39.90 an hour lands at $82,992.00, just $2,992.00 past $80,000.

The $100,000 Question: 7 Hours a Week Lands $212 Short

Six figures is the milestone every wage guide gets asked about. Here is the honest price of reaching it from $38 an hour. A $100,000 salary needs a $48.08-an-hour rate at 40 hours a week, which is $10.08 an hour above $38.00. With overtime alone, the gap is $20,960.00 of gross, and each overtime hour pays $57.00:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — The gap$100,000.00 − $79,040.00$20,960.00
Step 2 — Overtime hours needed$20,960.00 ÷ $57.00367.72 hours a year
Step 3 — Per week367.72 ÷ 52 weeks7.08 hours a week
Step 4 — The week that does it40.00 + 7.08 hours a week47.08-hour week
Step 5 — Take-home at $100,000Federal $13,170.00 + FICA $7,650.00 off $100,000.00$79,180.00

The cheaper road to six figures is usually the raise, not the hours. Each $1 raise keeps $1,463.28, so the $10.08 climb to $48.08 an hour is worth $14,749.86 of take-home with no extra hours at all. That is why the raise section of our 5%-raise guide is the better next read if the $100,000 line is your target. Round the overtime road to whole hours and a quirk shows up: 7 overtime hours a week, every week, is a $99,788.00 year and $79,030.86 of take-home, $212.00 short of six figures, while 8 overtime hours a week overshoots to $102,752.00 gross and $81,116.03 of take-home. No whole number of weekly overtime hours lands exactly on $100,000 from $38 an hour. The exact crossing is 368 overtime hours a year (7.08 a week), at $100,016.00 gross and $79,191.26 of take-home. But that is a 47-hour week, every week of the year, with no slow weeks and no cap on overtime. It is a different job than the occasional late finish, and the overtime premium is the only reason it works: those 368 hours at straight time would pay $13,984.00, not $20,976.00. Our $50-an-hour guide crosses six figures on straight time alone, at $104,000.00 gross.

Is $38 an Hour a Good Wage?

Set $38 next to the country and it clears the bar with room to spare. The median hourly wage runs roughly $24.51 an hour, or $50,980.80 a year. So $38 sits $13.49 an hour, or 55.0%, above the median, worth $28,059.20 a year more than the median worker’s full-time gross. It also pays 5.24 times the $7.25 federal minimum wage, and it equals 101.7% of the BLS average hourly earnings for private-sector workers (about $37.38 an hour in early 2026). Just above the average, well above the middle. By the usual “above median” test, $38 is good pay.

The monthly test tells you more. Federal-only take-home is $5,369.55 a month. Run the 50/30/20 budget on that $5,369.55 and it splits into $2,684.78 for needs, $1,610.87 for wants, and $1,073.91 for savings and extra debt payments. That split works, as long as the needs column stays honest about state tax and health premiums. Apply the common 30% rent rule and the rent budget comes to $1,610.87 a month. That budget works in most mid-size cities and gets tight in the priciest ones, which is why one wage can feel like two. Two cautions before you call it good. The $5,369.55 needs a full 40-hour week all year, no unpaid weeks, and no state tax. It also assumes no 401(k) or health premium comes off first. A 5% 401(k) contribution takes $3,952.00 a year and costs $3,082.56 of take-home after the $869.44 federal saving ($256.88 a month, $118.56 a biweekly check), as our 401(k)-paycheck guide prices in dollars. One milestone to keep in sight: $10,000 of spending money takes 322.79 take-home hours (8.07 weeks), not the 263.16 gross hours the rate alone suggests. Our $30-an-hour guide and $37-an-hour guide run these same benchmarks at their rates, so you can see where $38 sits on the whole ladder.

What $38 an Hour Keeps in 5 States

Every take-home figure above is federal only. Your state takes the next bite, and it is the biggest single gap between two workers on the same $38 rate. This table runs the same $79,040 year through five states, using the state tables in our paycheck calculator. Federal tax ($8,558.80) and FICA ($6,046.56) stay the same in every row. Only the state line moves:

StateState income taxTake-home after federal + stateTake-home per month
Texas (no state income tax)$0.00$64,434.64$5,369.55
Pennsylvania (flat 3.07%)$2,426.53$62,008.11$5,167.34
California (progressive)$3,146.32$61,288.32$5,107.36
New York (progressive)$3,671.16$60,763.48$5,063.62
Illinois (flat 4.95%)$3,912.48$60,522.16$5,043.51

Pennsylvania is the cheapest of the four taxing states here. Its flat 3.07% on all wages comes to $2,426.53, while Illinois charges its flat 4.95% the same way and lands highest at $3,912.48. California and New York sit in the middle because their progressive rates start low, and only the top slice of this income reaches their higher brackets. The spread is real money. Texas keeps $3,912.48 a year more than Illinois on the same job, which is $326.04 a month or $150.48 on every biweekly check. Two honest notes before you move for a tax rate. First, these are state estimates only. Local taxes stay out, so a New York City worker or a Pennsylvania worker with a local earned-income tax keeps less than the table shows. Second, the state line does not change your federal tax here, because this sketch uses the standard deduction and does not itemize state tax. Our paycheck calculator runs these same state tables on any rate, so you can price your own state before you compare offers.

Two $38-an-Hour Years That Don’t Look Alike

The $79,040 headline assumes the same 40-hour week, 52 weeks a year. Real $38-an-hour jobs rarely look like that. Here are two common ones, priced the same way as the rest of this guide:

YearHoursAnnual grossFederal-only take-homeTake-home per month
Straight time (baseline)40 hrs × 52 wks$79,040.00$64,434.64$5,369.55
School-year worker40 hrs × 40 wks$60,800.00$51,032.80$4,252.73
Night-shift worker20 hrs at $38 + 20 hrs at $41$82,160.00$66,629.56$5,552.46

The night-shift worker is the better-paid version of the same rate. Half the week at the $38.00 base and half at $41.00 with a $3.00 night differential pays $1,580.00 a week, or $82,160.00 a year, and keeps $66,629.56. That is $3,120.00 more gross and $2,194.92 more take-home than the straight-time year, and each $3.00 differential hour keeps $2.11 after federal tax and FICA. The differential is worth about the same as a $1.50 raise on every hour, with no extra hours at all. The school-year worker is the quieter story. A school bus driver or cafeteria worker on a 40-week school calendar earns $60,800.00 gross and keeps $51,032.80 after federal tax alone, which is $4,252.73 a month. The summer off costs $18,240.00 of gross and $13,401.84 of take-home against the full year, yet that shorter year still beats a $60,000 salary by $800.00 gross and $642.80 of take-home, because the salary comparison uses the same federal method.

Run the $38 Numbers for Your Own Week

Your own week, priced in four steps:

  1. Step 1: rate and paid weeks. Type $38 into the hourly-to-salary calculator with your real hours per week and your real paid weeks. Do not leave it at 52 by default if some weeks go unpaid.
  2. Step 2: your schedule. Try the schedules from the table (20, 25, 30, 35, or 37.5 hours) and watch gross pay move before you compare any offers.
  3. Step 3: overtime. Add overtime in the overtime calculator only if your role offers it, and use hours you have verified, not hours you hope for.
  4. Step 4: the salary rival. Work both offers out as yearly pay on paid weeks, then price benefits in dollars before you decide.

Where These Estimates Stop

  1. Federal only unless stated: these take-home figures follow 2026 federal rules for a single filer who takes the $16,100 standard deduction. State and local taxes are not in them, so a real paycheck lands lower in most states.
  2. A full-time year is assumed: the $79,040.00 headline needs 40 paid hours in all 52 weeks. Fewer hours, unpaid weeks, and seasonal gaps all pull it down. The schedules and unpaid-weeks tables price exactly how much.
  3. Overtime is not guaranteed: every overtime figure here assumes the extra hours exist and pay time and a half. Exempt workers get no overtime premium, and some employers cap overtime hours.
  4. The 22% slice fits this rate only: the $12,540.00 figure rests on $79,040.00 of gross and the $16,100 standard deduction. A 401(k) contribution, a different filing status, or a second income moves where the bracket line falls.
  5. Benefits sit outside the salary math: health premiums, 401(k) matches, and paid time off stay out of the salary comparisons unless a note says otherwise. A strong benefits package can flip the $75,000 and $80,000 rows.
  6. Rounding: per-check figures round to the cent. A rounded monthly figure times 12 can land a few cents away from the annual figure.
  7. Not tax or legal advice: these are 2026 federal estimates for a single filer who takes the standard deduction, built the same way as the site’s other guides. Your employer’s payroll calendar, withholding choices, and benefit deductions will change the figures.

Frequently Asked Questions

The questions readers ask most about $38 an hour, answered straight:

How much is $38 an hour biweekly?

Before taxes, $38 an hour pays $3,040 every two weeks (80 hours × $38). After federal tax and FICA alone, a single filer keeps $2,478.26 per biweekly paycheck ($64,434.64 ÷ 26). Don’t mix up biweekly and semi-monthly: semi-monthly gross is $3,293.33 (24 paychecks), and semi-monthly take-home is $2,684.78. The totals still match because two months of the year carry three biweekly paychecks while the other ten carry two.

How much is $38 an hour per month?

The exact average is $6,586.67 gross a month ($79,040 ÷ 12), and $5,369.55 take-home after federal tax alone for a single filer. You’ll see two shortcuts online, and both are a bit off: multiplying the weekly figure by 4 gives $6,080, which is a short month, and multiplying by 4.33 gives $6,581.60. Both use a different year length than the standard 2,080-hour year this guide uses.

How much is $38 an hour after taxes?

For a single filer in 2026 taking the standard deduction, take-home after federal tax alone is $64,434.64 a year. That’s $79,040 gross minus $8,558.80 federal income tax (10% × $12,400 + 12% × $38,000 + 22% × $12,540) minus $6,046.56 FICA. It works out to $5,369.55 a month, $2,478.26 biweekly, or $30.98 kept from each hour. State income tax, retirement contributions, and health premiums aren’t in that number, so a real paycheck will be lower.

Is $38 an hour good pay?

Nationally, yes. It sits 55.0% above the median hourly wage of roughly $24.51 an hour, which works out to $50,980.80 a year, a gap of $28,059.20. It’s also 101.7% of the BLS average hourly earnings for private-sector workers (about $37.38 an hour in early 2026), so it’s just above the average and well above the middle, and 5.24 times the $7.25 federal minimum wage. Whether it feels good depends on your hours, household size, and city: $5,369.55 a month of federal-only take-home puts the 30% rent budget at $1,610.87, comfortable in most mid-size cities and tight in the most expensive ones.

How much is $38 an hour part-time?

At 25 hours a week all year, $38 an hour is $49,400 gross and $41,872.90 take-home after federal tax alone for a single filer. At 20 hours a week it’s $39,520 gross and $33,934.32 take-home, the same figures as a $19-an-hour full-time year, because the gross is identical. Part-time take-home keeps a slightly higher share of gross (85.9% at 20 hours, against 81.5% full-time) because less income reaches the 22% bracket. Check the schedules table for every step from 20 to 40 hours.

What salary is $38 an hour equal to?

At a standard full-time year, $38 an hour equals a $79,040 salary. That’s $960 a year below an $80,000 salary, and $675.36 below it after federal tax alone ($64,434.64 against $65,110.00). The gap closes with 17 overtime hours a year at $57.00 an hour, as the $80,000-salary section shows. Paid weeks can flip the comparison, though: with two unpaid weeks the hourly job falls to $76,000 gross and trails an $80,000 salary by $4,000, so always compare on paid weeks, not on the headline rate.

Key Takeaways & Action Plan

  • $38 an hour is $79,040 a year full-time: $1,520 a week, $3,040 biweekly, $6,587 a month on average, before taxes.
  • Federal-only take-home is $64,434.64 for a single filer: $5,369.55 a month, $2,478.26 biweekly, $30.98 kept per hour, at a 22% marginal rate.
  • $12,540 of your income reaches the 22% bracket. The 22% rate costs $2,758.80, which is why your effective federal rate is 10.8%, not 22%.
  • A $1 raise from here keeps exactly $1,463.28. The figure stays flat from $32 an hour up to about $58.56 an hour, where the 24% bracket starts.
  • Five overtime hours a week add $14,820 a year ($93,860 total; $74,860.51 take-home), if the hours are real and you are non-exempt.
  • 17 overtime hours a year close the $80,000 gap. About twenty minutes a week puts the hourly year past an $80,000 salary.
  • Seven overtime hours a week land $212 short of $100,000 ($99,788 gross), while eight a week overshoot to $102,752. No whole weekly number lands exactly on six figures.
  • Two unpaid weeks cost $3,040 gross ($2,138.64 take-home). That loss beats the whole $37-to-$38 raise, and it turns a $4,040 lead over a $75,000 salary into a $1,000 deficit. Compare on paid weeks and real hours, not the headline rate.

Sources & Method

How we got these numbers. Gross pay uses the standard full-time year of 2,080 hours (40 hours × 52 weeks). Monthly figures divide the annual total by 12. Biweekly figures use 26 paychecks. The after-tax sketch follows 2026 federal rules for a single filer who takes the standard deduction: a $16,100 standard deduction, then brackets of 10% to $12,400, 12% to $50,400, and 22% to $105,700 of taxable income, per IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-32. FICA runs 7.65% (Social Security 6.2% up to the $184,500 wage base, Medicare 1.45%), and this income sits below the wage base. The median wage comes from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics, May 2025 ($24.51 an hour). Average hourly earnings for private-sector workers ran about $37.38 an hour in early 2026 (BLS, via ClimbTheLadder). Cross-checks tie this guide to its neighbors: the $60,000-salary take-home of $50,390.00 matches the site’s $60,000 guide; the $70,000-salary take-home of $58,075.00 matches the $32 and $33 guides; the $75,000-salary take-home of $61,592.50 matches the $36 guide; the $80,000-salary take-home of $65,110.00 matches the $36 guide’s nearby table; the $100,000 take-home of $79,180.00 matches the $100,000 guide; the $39-an-hour take-home of $65,897.92 comes from this same method and will tie out when the $39 guide is written. Competitor check: FinalRoundAI gives the $79,040 gross and $64,434.64 take-home with bracket steps in its detail section, then contradicts itself on the monthly figure ($5,332.55 in one place against the correct $5,369.55) and claims federal plus FICA “can take over $16,100” at this wage, when the real total is $14,605.36. DollarCalcs gives the $79,040 gross and $64,435 take-home with a six-state table, but calls the 18.5% combined federal-plus-FICA rate the “effective federal rate” (the federal rate alone is 10.8%) and prices no raise, overtime, or unpaid-week cases. WageMetric’s after-tax range tops out at $63,508.64, below the correct federal-only figure, and its page is stale (published January 2026). SalaryConverter runs a flat 25% tax and lands on $60,551.64 of take-home, $3,883.00 below the real figure. SureCalcs gives $64,435 with correct bracket steps but no overtime, unpaid-week, or raise cases. This article is general information, not tax or legal advice.

3 Things to Remember

  1. The headline is $79,040 gross and $64,434.64 kept after federal tax alone, or $5,369.55 a month for a single filer.
  2. Only $12,540 of your income reaches the 22% bracket, so a $1 raise from here keeps exactly $1,463.28, and 17 overtime hours close the gap to an $80,000 salary.
  3. Hours, paid weeks, and overtime move the year more than the rate does: 30 hours pays $59,280, two unpaid weeks cost $3,040, and five overtime hours add $14,820.

Methodology & Data Verification

  • Basis: Pay figures are gross unless a section states take-home; tax figures use 2026 federal rules where shown.
  • Method: Full formulas, baselines, and rounding rules are on our calculation methodology page.
  • Coverage: U.S. federal rules; state and local rules vary and are not included.
  • Review: Last updated November 26, 2026.
  • Disclaimer: Estimates for planning only — not tax or legal advice.
